{{Short description|Ability to easily switch cryptographic primitives}}
In [[cryptographic protocol]] design, '''cryptographic agility''' or '''crypto-agility''' is the ability to switch between multiple [[cryptographic primitive]]s.

A cryptographically agile system implementing a particular standard can choose which combination of primitives to use. The primary goal of cryptographic agility is to enable rapid adaptations of new [[cryptographic primitive]]s and [[encryption|algorithms]] without making disruptive changes to the system's infrastructure.

Cryptographic agility acts as a safety measure or an incident response mechanism for when a cryptographic primitive of a system is discovered to be vulnerable.<ref name="JasmineHenry-what-is">{{cite web |last1=Henry |first1=Jasmine |title=What is Crypto-Agility? |url=https://www.cryptomathic.com/news-events/blog/what-is-crypto-agility |publisher=Cryptomathic |accessdate=26 November 2018}}</ref> A security system is considered crypto-agile if its cryptographic algorithms or parameters can be replaced with ease and is at least partly automated.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://crypto.stanford.edu/RealWorldCrypto/slides/kenny.pdf|title=Key Reuse: Theory and Practice (Workshop on Real-World Cryptography)|last1=Patterson |first1=Kenny|publisher=Stanford University|accessdate=26 November 2018}}</ref><ref name="Microsoft-Crypto-Agility">{{cite web|url=http://media.blackhat.com/bh-us-10/whitepapers/Sullivan/BlackHat-USA-2010-Sullivan-Cryptographic-Agility-wp.pdf|title=Cryptographic Agility|last1=Sullivan|first1=Bryan|publisher=Microsoft Corporation on Blackhat.com|accessdate=26 November 2018}}</ref> The impending arrival of a [[Quantum computing|quantum computer]] that can break existing [[Public-key cryptography|asymmetric cryptography]] is raising awareness of the importance of cryptographic agility.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Better Safe Than Sorry: Preparing for Crypto-Agility|url=https://www.gartner.com/en/documents/3645384/better-safe-than-sorry-preparing-for-crypto-agility|access-date=2020-10-19|website=Gartner|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Steel|first=Graham|date=2019-01-21|title=Achieving Crypto Agility|url=https://cryptosense.com/blog/achieving-crypto-agility/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200805020632/https://cryptosense.com/blog/achieving-crypto-agility/ |archive-date=2020-08-05 |access-date=2020-10-19|website=Cryptosense|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Example==
The [[X.509]] [[public key certificate]] illustrates crypto-agility. A public key certificate has [[cryptography|cryptographic parameters]] including key type, key length, and a [[hash function|hash algorithm]]. X.509 version v.3, with key type RSA, a 1024-bit key length, and the SHA-1 hash algorithm were found by [[NIST]] to have a key length that made it vulnerable to attacks, thus prompting the transition to SHA-2.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.csoonline.com/article/2879073/all-you-need-to-know-about-the-move-from-sha1-to-sha2-encryption.html|title=All you need to know about the move from SHA1 to SHA2 encryption|last=Grimes|first=Roger A.|date=2017-07-06|website=CSO Online|language=en|access-date=2019-05-19}}</ref>

==Importance==
With the rise of [[Transport Layer Security|secure transport layer communication]] in the end of the 1990s, cryptographic primitives and algorithms have been increasingly popular; for example, by 2019, more than 80% of all websites employed some form of security measures.<ref>{{cite web |title=How Let's Encrypt doubled the internet's percentage of secure websites in four years |url=https://news.umich.edu/how-lets-encrypt-doubled-the-internets-percentage-of-secure-websites-in-four-years/ |website=University of Michigan News |date=13 November 2019}}</ref> Furthermore, cryptographic techniques are widely incorporated to protect applications and business transactions.

However, as cryptographic algorithms are deployed, research of their security intensifies, and new attacks against cryptographic primitives (old and new alike) are discovered. Crypto-agility tries to tackle the implied threat to information security by allowing swift deprecation of vulnerable primitives and replacement with new ones.

This threat is not merely theoretical; many algorithms that were once considered secure ([[Data Encryption Standard|DES]], 512-bit [[RSA (cryptosystem)|RSA]], [[RC4]]) are now known to be vulnerable, some even to amateur attackers. On the other hand, new algorithms ([[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]], [[Elliptic Curve Cryptography|Elliptic curve cryptography]]) are often both more secure and faster in comparison to old ones. Systems designed to meet crypto-agility criteria are expected to be less affected should current primitives be found vulnerable, and may enjoy better [[latency (engineering)|latency]] or battery usage by using new and improved primitives.
 
For example, [[quantum computing]], if feasible, is expected to be able to defeat existing public key cryptography algorithms. The overwhelming majority of existing public-key infrastructure relies on the computational hardness of problems such as [[integer factorization]] and [[discrete logarithm|discrete logarithms]] (which includes [[elliptic-curve cryptography]] as a special case). Quantum computers running [[Shor's algorithm]] can solve these problems exponentially faster than the best-known algorithms for conventional computers.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://blogs.ams.org/mathgradblog/2014/04/30/shors-algorithm-breaking-rsa-encryption/|title=Shor's Algorithm – Breaking RSA Encryption|last1=Bl|first1=Stephanie|last2=a|date=2014-05-01|website=AMS Grad Blog|language=en-US|access-date=2019-08-09}}</ref> [[Post-quantum cryptography]] is the subfield of cryptography that aims to replace quantum-vulnerable algorithms with new ones that are believed hard to break even for a quantum computer. The main families of post-quantum alternatives to factoring and discrete logarithms include [[lattice-based cryptography]], [[multivariate cryptography]], [[hash-based cryptography]], and [[Post-quantum_cryptography#Code-based_cryptography|code-based cryptography]].

==Awareness==
System evolution and crypto-agility are not the same. System evolution progresses on the basis of emerging business and technical requirements. Crypto-agility is related instead to computing infrastructure and requires consideration by security experts, system designers, and application developers.<ref name="Jasminehenry-3DES">{{cite web |last1=Henry |first1=Jasmine |title=3DES is Officially Being Retired |url=https://www.cryptomathic.com/news-events/blog/3des-is-officially-being-retired |publisher=Cryptomathic |accessdate=26 November 2018}}</ref> 

==Best practices==
Best practices about dealing with crypto-agility include:<ref name="AsimMehmood-crypto-agility">{{cite web |last1=Mehmood |first1=Asim |title=What is crypto-agility and how to achieve it? |url=https://content.hsm.utimaco.com/blog/what-is-crypto-agility-and-how-to-achieve-it |publisher=Utimaco |accessdate=26 November 2018 |archive-date=27 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190327221802/https://content.hsm.utimaco.com/blog/what-is-crypto-agility-and-how-to-achieve-it |url-status=dead }}</ref>

* All business applications involving any sort of cryptographic technology should incorporate the latest algorithms and techniques.
* Crypto-agility requirements must be disseminated to all hardware, software, and service suppliers, who must comply on a timely basis; suppliers who cannot address these requirements must be replaced.
* Suppliers must provide timely updates and identify the crypto technology they employ.
* Quantum-resistant solutions should be kept in mind.<ref name="NIST Post-Quantum">{{cite web |last1=Chen |first1=Lily |last2=Jordan |first2=Stephen |last3=Liu |first3=Yi-Kai |last4=Moody |first4=Dustin |last5=Peralta |first5=Rene |last6=Perlner |first6=Ray |last7=Smith-Tone |first7=Daniel |title=Report on Post-Quantum Cryptography (NISTIR 8105) |url=https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2016/nist.ir.8105.pdf |publisher=National Institute of Standards and Technology NIST |accessdate=26 November 2018}}</ref>
* [[Symmetric-key algorithm|Symmetric-key algorithms]] should be flexible in their key lengths.
* Hash algorithms should support different lengths of outputs.
* Digital certificate and private key rotations must be automated.<ref name="Digital certificate and private key rotations must be automated.">{{cite web|url=https://zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_c_zTCRI0QZ6SI01MazDbNg|title=Digital certificate and private key rotations must be automated.|website=www.appviewx.com|access-date=20 April 2020}}{{Dead link|date=December 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>
* Standards and regulations must be complied with.<ref name="Cryptographic Agility in Practice: Emerging USe-cases">{{cite web |last1=Macaulay |first1=Tyson |title=Cryptographic Agility in Practice |url=https://uploads-ssl.webflow.com/5bd73d456f7b3f2db2bbbb95/5c76a740dcc2cc4646a06805_ISG_AgilityUseCases_Whitepaper-FINAL.pdf |publisher=InfoSec Global |accessdate=5 March 2019}}</ref>
* The names of the algorithms used should be communicated and not assumed or defaulted.

==Other designs==
Cryptographic agility typically increases the complexity of the applications that rely on it. Developers need to build support for each of the optional cryptographic primitives, introducing more code and increasing the chance of implementation flaws as well as increasing maintenance and support costs.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imperialviolet.org/2016/05/16/agility.html|title=Cryptographic Agility|first1=Adam|last1=Langley|access-date=2025-02-07}}</ref> Users of the systems need to select which primitives they wish to use; for example, [[OpenSSL]] users can select from dozens of ciphersuites when using [[Transport_Layer_Security|TLS]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://docs.openssl.org/3.4/man1/openssl-ciphers/#cipher-suite-names|title=OpenSSL 3.4 Cipher Suite Names|access-date=2025-02-07}}</ref> Further, when two parties negotiate the cryptographic primitives for their message exchange, it creates the opportunity for downgrade attacks by intermediaries (such as [[POODLE]]), or for the selection of insecure primitives.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://auth0.com/blog/critical-vulnerabilities-in-json-web-token-libraries/|title=Critical vulnerabilities in JSON Web Token libraries|first1=Tim|last1=McLean|access-date=2025-02-07}}</ref>

One alternative approach is to dramatically limit the choices available to both developers and users, so that there is less scope for implementation or configuration flaws.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.blockchaincommons.com/musings/musings-agility/|title=Musings of a Trust Architect: Problems of Cryptographic Agility|first1=Christopher|last1=Allen|date=8 March 2023 |access-date=2025-02-07}}</ref> In this approach, the designers of the library or system choose the primitives and do not offer a choice of cryptographic primitives (or, if they do, it is a very constrained set of choices). Opinionated encryption is visible in tools like [[NaCl_(software)#Libsodium|Libsodium]], where high-level APIs explicitly aim to discourage developers from picking primitives, and in [[WireGuard]], where single primitives are picked to intentionally eliminate crypto-agility.<ref>{{cite web|last=Donenfeld|first=Jason|access-date=2025-02-07|title=WireGuard: Next Generation Kernel Network Tunnel|url=https://www.wireguard.com/papers/wireguard.pdf|website=Wireguard.com}}</ref>

If opinionated encryption is used and a vulnerability is discovered in one of the primitives in a protocol, there is no way to substitute better primitives. Instead, the solution is to use versioned protocols. A new version of the protocol will include the fixed primitive. As a consequence of this, two parties running different versions of the protocol will not be able to communicate.

==Agility as a generalized design principle==
[[Quantum cryptography]]—and more broadly, Physical Layer Security (PLS)—exploit physical processes for cryptographic purposes and are inherently hardware-dependent. This has motivated the development of a conceptual framework for agility as a generalized design principle applicable to hardware systems and extending beyond cryptography.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Galambos |first1=Máté |last2=Vázquez-Castro |first2=Ángeles |last3=Bacsárdi |first3=László |chapter=Hardware Supported Crypto-Agility in Quantum Key Distribution and Physical Layer Security |date=2025-05-19 |title=2025 IEEE 19th International Symposium on Applied Computational Intelligence and Informatics (SACI) |publisher=IEEE |pages=000069–000074 |doi=10.1109/SACI66288.2025.11030148 |isbn=979-8-3315-1547-8}}</ref> The framework emphasizes '''functional components''' that rather than traditional cryptographic primitives. These components may be hardware, software, or organizational units, and are characterized by processing an input <math>x</math> to produce an output <math>y=f(x)</math>. The nature of <math>x</math> depends on context: it may represent data in software systems, electronic or optical signals in hardware, or even be absent in some scenarios.

An agile functional component is capable of producing the output <math>y</math> through multiple distinct <math>f_1(x), f_2(x), f_3(x)...</math> processes, where these functions must simultaneously satisfy three key conditions:<ref name=":0" />

# '''Interchangeability''': The <math>f_1(x), f_2(x), f_3(x)...</math> processes must be sufficiently similar to fulfill the same intended purpose. (For instance, a hardware component might be designed to generate random numbers in a variety of ways, allowing for alternative implementations that can perform equivalent tasks.)
# '''Diversity''': The realized <math>f_1(x), f_2(x), f_3(x)...</math> processes should exhibit meaningful distinctions. (These differences could be independent failure modes, vulnerabilities, varying trade-offs, or different operating ranges, etc., ensuring that the system remains robust under changing conditions.)
# '''Switchability''': The cost associated with transitioning between these <math>f_1(x), f_2(x), f_3(x)...</math> processes should be sufficiently low. (Such costs could be quantified in terms of time, financial resources, or administrative overhead, etc., and should not significantly impact the end user of the system.)

Ideally, the design specifications of an agile system would explicitly define the cost metrics and criteria for interchangeability, diversity, and switchability.<ref name=":0" />

Several strategies enhance hardware agility, including flexible signal routing between subcomponents, parallelization and duplication of subcomponents, use of pluggable/swappable subcomponents, and multifunctional subcomponents.<ref name=":0" />
